summary: Research + fact-check the volley, then draft, judge, critique and finalize the storyboard and narration for the 3-kick explainer

research.kick: Volley and half-volley: a first-time laces strike on a dropping ball (volley) or on a ball that has just bounced (half-volley), kept low or made to dip under the bar with topspin.
research.one_line_hook: Near your foot the ball drops 1 cm every 2 thousandths of a second, and you get one 9-millisecond touch. Here is how strikers make it dive under the bar.
research.mechanism_story:
Step 1, see it drop. The ball falls toward you. Near knee height it moves at about 20 km/h. Good strikers look ahead to where it will arrive. Then they turn the head with it.

Step 2, set early. Put the standing foot beside the spot where the ball will be. Point its toes at the target.

Step 3, swing before it arrives. The last whip of the leg, from full knee bend to the hit, takes about 70 thousandths of a second. In that time a ball dropped from head height falls another 30-40 cm. That is more than the ball's own width. So you start the whip while the ball is still well over your foot.

Step 4, hit a tiny target. Near the foot, the ball falls 1 cm in about 2 thousandths of a second. Meet it 1-2 cm lower and it takes off several degrees higher. From the edge of the box, the whole goal is only about 8 degrees tall.

Step 5, close the face. Your laces act like a tennis racket face. Knee over the ball, toes down and a locked ankle tilt the face forward and down. Lean back and the face tilts up. Only 5 degrees of tilt puts the ball 1.4 m higher at a goal 16 m away.

Step 6, the touch. Foot and ball touch for about 9 thousandths of a second. The falling ball slides down your laces, grips and rolls forward over the top. Forward spin comes almost for free.

Step 7, the dive. A ball that rolls forward flicks air up off its back. The air pushes back and shoves the ball down. At 90 km/h with 4 turns each second, this push is about half the ball's weight. Spin push plus Earth's pull makes the dip. From 16 m, the ball arrives about 1.3 m lower than the same shot with no spin.

Step 8, why smashing it fails. A faster ball reaches the goal sooner, so Earth's pull has less time to bring it down. A take-off angle that scores at 72 km/h can clear the bar at 90 km/h.

Step 9, why the half-volley helps. You can see the bounce spot coming, at a known height. Certified turf also takes 35-45% of the ball's speed, so it rises slower than it fell. At the very top of a bounce, the ball stays less than 1 cm from its highest point for about 90 thousandths of a second.

Step 10, the landing. If the dipping ball bounces in front of the keeper, its forward spin keeps about three quarters of its forward speed. It skids on.
plain_metaphors: Laces = tennis racket face. Tilt the face up (lean back) and the ball climbs. Tilt it forward and down (knee over the ball, toes down) and the ball stays low.

Raindrop vs soap bubble: a ball falling onto your foot is a raindrop (it moves 1 cm in about 2 thousandths of a second). A ball at the top of its bounce is a bubble that hangs for about 90 thousandths of a second.
Fist at arm's length: from the edge of the box, the whole goal looks less than one fist tall (about 8 degrees). One degree of error moves the ball about 28 cm at the goal line.
Wheel down a ramp: the falling ball slides down your laces, grips and rolls forward, like a wheel that rolls down a ramp. It leaves already spinning forward.
Paddle wheel: a forward-rolling ball throws air up off its back. Throw air up and the air shoves you down.
Double-gravity button: at about 97 km/h with 7 turns each second, the spin push is about as big as the ball's own weight. For that ball, it is like switching gravity to double.
Car over a jump: a faster car flies further before it lands. A harder volley also flies further before Earth's pull brings it down, so it clears the bar.
Pendulum vs door: a front-on swing moves like a pendulum, so bad timing sends the ball too high or too low. A side-on swing moves like a door, so bad timing sends it left or right.
Camera on a tripod: keep your head still like a camera on a tripod. Turn it smoothly with the ball, and the ball stays in the middle of the picture.
Pre-marked spot: in a half-volley the bounce is like a dot painted on the grass. You know where and how high the ball will be.
Tennis return: a hard serve comes back faster, but only part of the serve's speed returns. An oncoming ball adds only about a fifth to two fifths of its speed to your shot.
Accidental chip: a short stab under a volley is the chip action by mistake. The ball gets backspin and floats up.

claims.claim: Definitions: a volley is struck first-time as the ball drops out of the air. A ball hit on the bounce is a half-volley. Volleys are 'a highly technical finish'.
US Youth Soccer curriculum: 'introduce half volley & volley shooting' at U12, and 'half volley & volley shooting' at U14.

US Youth Soccer half-volley instep cues: plant foot alongside the ball as it bounces, 'keep the head and knee over it', 'try to hit the ball when it is no more than 2" off the ground', 'toes down and curled back', raise the knee on the follow-through to keep it under the bar.

US Youth Soccer volley instep cues: let the ball drop below knee height, hip and knee over the ball, hit at or slightly above the ball's middle line to keep it low, toes down, ankle locked, 'watch the foot connect with the ball', look up only after the kicking foot is back on the ground. Backswing shorter than for a ground ball.
claims.value: contact at or just above the middle

claims.claim: US Youth Soccer side volley: upper body bent sideways over the support leg 'almost horizontal', knee well up to direct the ball down, strike at or above the middle line, 'the greater the extent of the turn on the standing (axis) leg the more power'. Ball struck above the middle line 'will be propelled downward'.

Side-on volley cues (Soccer Coach Weekly): 'Upper body falls away from ball', 'Knee moves through ahead of the ball', 'Contact ball above horizontal midline', 'Body rotates around non-kicking leg', leg swings 'almost parallel with the ground'.

Volley drill cues: 'Head and knee over the ball to keep the volley down', 'Lock ankle, point toes down, use laces', 'Let the ball fall as low as possible', 'Strike middle to bottom half of ball but not underneath'. Throw, bounce and volley from about 20 yards, adjusted for age.

Failed volleys (over the goal) vs good ones: 10 university players at 500 Hz. In failures the foot hit the bottom part of the ball, with less hip turn-in during the backswing, a more upright foot at impact and a more downward leg swing just before impact. Failure patterns differed between players.

Volleys at 0, 25, 50 and 75 cm ball heights (15 players, 500 Hz): upward foot speed comes from knee bend, thigh turn-in, sideways hip tilt and hip flexion. Turn-in and hip tilt grow as the ball gets higher.
Kicking a rolling ball vs a stationary ball (9 skilled players): no significant difference in foot speed at contact or leg motion.

Moving-ball kicks (8 experienced, 10 less experienced): no difference in peak foot speed between groups or conditions. Experienced players were more accurate. The time from peak hip angle to contact was longer for a moving ball.
Machine-served volleys at 9.0, 11.5 and 15.0 m/s (9 players): ball speed tracked foot speed in every condition. The ball-to-foot speed ratio was highest when the ball met the middle of the foot.
Timing of a maximal instep kick (20 elite players): backswing 0.112 s, leg cocking 0.072 s, final whip from max knee bend to impact 0.070 +/- 0.007 s, whole kick 0.603 s.

OWN CALCULATION: a ball dropped from 1.5-2 m reaches knee height (0.4 m) at 4.7-5.6 m/s (17-20 km/h). In the last 70 ms before contact it falls 30-37 cm. In the last 142 ms it falls 56-70 cm. It moves 1 cm in about 1.8-2.2 ms.

OWN CALCULATION: at the top of a bounce the ball stays less than 1 cm from its highest point for about 90 ms (45 ms each side), and less than 2 cm for about 130 ms. That is about 25 times more forgiving than a ball falling at 20 km/h.

FIFA turf test: a ball dropped from 2 m rebounds 0.60-0.85 m (from earlier verified research). OWN CONVERSION: it leaves the turf at 55-65% of its landing speed. A ball dropped from waist height (1 m) bounces to about 30-42 cm and rises at about 2.4-2.9 m/s.
Players meet the ball about 10 mm below centre for a high target and near the centre for a low target (7 players, 42 trials). Earlier verified research.
claims.value: 1 cm on the ball = high vs low

claims.claim: A finite-element model gives the fastest ball from contact 2-4 cm below centre, with a maximum take-off angle of 16 degrees at 2 cm below centre (Asai 2005, in the Lees review). Earlier verified research.

OWN MODEL (point mass, contact 0.4 m, goal 16 m): the take-off angles that put the ball under a 2.44 m bar span only about 8 degrees (about 7 degrees for a 2.13 m youth bar). Geometry: 1 degree = 28 cm at 16 m, 5 degrees = 1.4 m.

OWN MODEL: with no spin from 16 m, the scoring window is about 12-21 degrees at 72 km/h but about 7-15 degrees at 90 km/h. A harder hit at the same angle flies higher at the goal line, because it has less time to fall (0.7 s vs 0.9 s).

OWN MODEL: with 4 turns per second of topspin at 90 km/h, the ball arrives about 1.25-1.3 m lower at 16 m than a no-spin ball launched at the same angle (about 1.6 m lower at 72 km/h). The scoring window shifts up by about 5 degrees. The window does not get wider. Volley spin rates are an assumption: none are measured.

Spin force size: Asai 2007 found a side-force coefficient of about 0.25 at 27 m/s and 7 rev/s (verified earlier). OWN ARITHMETIC: that gives about 4.1 N, about the ball's 4.2 N weight. At 25 m/s and 4 rev/s the model gives about 2.5 N, about half to two thirds of the weight.
Launcher trajectory tests used pure backspin or pure topspin. Lift points along the spin-cross-velocity direction, so topspin pushes down. C_L is about 0.35 at spin parameter 0.5 and 14 m/s.

Bush (MIT): the 'Folha Seca' is struck with nearly pure topspin by brushing over the ball and 'dips dramatically'. 'While volleying a ball with topspin is relatively straightforward, imparting pure topspin is extremely difficult to do from a dead ball.'

OWN RIGID-BALL ESTIMATE: a ball falling at 4-5.6 m/s, struck by a level foot, slides down the laces and grips. It keeps about 60% of its fall speed as downward motion and leaves about 5-10 degrees below the push line with about 3.5-5 rev/s of topspin. If the foot rises faster than the ball falls, the grip gives backspin. Supported in principle by the slide-then-grip behaviour of obliquely hit balls.

OWN CALCULATION: head-on, the shot speed = (1.17-1.39) x foot speed + (0.17-0.39) x oncoming ball speed. This uses an effective foot mass of 1.7-2.1 kg (machine limb, earlier verified) and foot-ball bounciness 0.46-0.68. A 10 m/s oncoming ball adds only about 2-4 m/s. A ball moving away subtracts the same share. A ball falling across the swing adds almost nothing: closing speed is about 20.8 m/s for a 20 m/s foot and a 5.6 m/s drop.

Earlier verified facts that apply to laces volleys: contact about 9 ms; a locked ankle gave about 4% more ball speed in a machine; the fastest spot is the middle of the laces, about 6 cm in front of the ankle, and toe or ankle contact gave about 15% less speed; the shank is still speeding up at impact ('kick through the ball'); plant foot behind the ball makes it rise.
Kellis and Katis review: 'Accurate kicks are generally slower than powerful kicks.' Ball speed in maximal instep kicks ranges 18-35 m/s.
Youth shot speeds (earlier verified): about 67 km/h at U13, 77 km/h at U15, 81 km/h at U17. Ball/foot speed ratio rises from about 1.0 (U9) to 1.26 (U20).

Bahill and LaRitz 1984: a major-league batter tracked the pitch with eyes and head until about 5.5 ft (1.7 m) away, with eye speeds up to 120 deg/s. Other batters lost it at about 9 ft (2.7 m). One batter jumped his eyes ahead of the ball.

Mann, Spratford and Abernethy 2013: two elite cricket batters kept the head aimed within 2.4 +/- 1.7 degrees of the ball (club batters 3.7). Their gaze was on the bat-ball contact spot in 80-100% of trials. 'The ball could be followed if the batters simply moved their head and kept their eyes still.' 'The information at bat-ball contact was not necessary to make contact.'
Land and McLeod 2000: batsmen jump their eyes to where the ball will bounce, then follow it for about 100-200 ms after the bounce. A faster first eye jump went with better batting.

Quiet eye: the final steady look, held for at least 100 ms and within 3 degrees, before the final movement (Vickers). In soccer penalties it was longer in scored kicks (45 +/- 29%) than in missed kicks (18 +/- 10%).
People can intercept fast moving targets with very high timing precision, and adjust where rather than when they hit if given the choice. A value of about 5-6 ms comes from a search summary only.

OWN COUNT, StatsBomb open event data, 230 matches (2018 and 2022 World Cups, Euro 2020 and 2024): volleys 36 and half-volleys 60 of 507 non-penalty goals, about 1 in 5 (19%). Conversion: volleys 10.3% (350 shots), half-volleys 8.8% (685), normal foot shots about 8.4%.

OWN COUNT, same data: 54% of volleys and 45% of half-volleys missed the target (off target, wayward or post), vs 34% of normal foot shots. 21.5% of volleys went over the bar vs 17.2% of normal shots. Volleys came from closer: median 14.3 m vs 20.2 m.

Premier League 2008/09 (Durlik and Bieniek, cited by Shan): 69.3% of goals came from zero-possession (first-time) shots. Of 132 Puskas Award nominated goals 2009-2021, 56.1% were struck from airborne balls. 51.5% were struck facing goal, 31.8% side-facing, 16.7% back-facing. A side volley reaches sideways about 0.4 body heights per leg.

Solo wall drill: 'Start by standing a few feet from a wall, dropping the football in front of you and then volleying it as it bounces up', then move back and aim at spots on the wall. Keep 'both your head and knee over the ball' and avoid leaning back.
Bounce test (earlier verified, rubber mat): a ball landing with backspin kept about 38% of its forward speed. A ball with topspin kept about 75%.

technique_cues: Let it drop: for a front-on volley, wait until the ball is below knee height (US Youth Soccer).
Set early: plant the standing foot beside where the ball will land, toes at the target.
Nose over knee, knee over ball.
Toes down, ankle locked, hit with the middle of the laces.
Hit the top half: meet the ball on or just above its middle.
Short backswing, full swing through the ball. Do not jab at it.
About 70-80% power. Clean contact beats a big swing.
Head still, turn it with the ball. Watch it onto your laces.
Look up only after your kicking foot lands again (US Youth Soccer).
Half-volley: hit it as it leaves the grass, no more than about 5 cm up (US Youth Soccer: 2 inches).
Easiest first volley: hit it at the top of its bounce, where it hangs still.
Side-on for waist-high balls: lean your upper body away, swing flat like a door, pivot on the standing foot, knee up, contact above the middle.
Raise the kicking knee on the follow-through to keep the ball under the bar (US Youth Soccer).

common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The shin tilts back, so the laces face opens upward and the foot is still rising at contact. The foot meets the bottom of the ball, and the ball can pick up backspin that lifts it more. Only 5 degrees more take-off angle puts the ball 1.4 m higher at a goal 16 m away. The goal window from there is only about 8 degrees. In lab tests, failed volleys (over the goal) hit the bottom part of the ball.
common_mistakes.fix: Nose over knee, knee over ball, chest slightly forward. Hit the top half.

common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Two problems. A faster ball reaches the goal sooner, so Earth's pull has less time to bring it down. From 16 m the no-spin window moves from about 12-21 degrees at 72 km/h to about 7-15 degrees at 90 km/h. So a take-off angle that scores at 72 km/h clears the bar at 90 km/h. Also, a wild swing is harder to time when the ball moves 1 cm every 2 thousandths of a second. Research shows accurate kicks are generally slower than powerful ones.
common_mistakes.fix: Use about 70-80% power. Short backswing, smooth swing through. Score with contact, not with muscle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stabbing at it (short jab, foot slows or chops down and under)
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot is slowing at impact, so the ball leaves slower. In good kicks the shank is still speeding up at contact. A jab down and under the ball is the chip action: it gives backspin, and the spin push lifts the ball, so the volley floats up.
common_mistakes.fix: Kick through the ball. Finish with the foot toward the target and land on the kicking foot.

common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The body is still moving when the ball arrives. The low point of the swing is not under the ball, so the player reaches, leans back and meets the ball on the way up. Coaching guides note that a plant foot behind the ball makes it rise.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the drop early. Set the standing foot beside the landing spot first, then swing.

common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The ball pushes the loose foot further down and soaks up energy. In a kicking machine a locked ankle gave about 4% more ball speed. Toes up also tilts the laces face upward, so the ball climbs. Toe contact gave about 15% less speed than the middle of the laces.
common_mistakes.fix: Toes pointed down and curled, ankle locked, strike with the middle of the laces.

common_mistakes.mistake: Volleying front-on when the ball is too high
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: A front-on leg swings like a pendulum. To reach a high ball, the foot must be rising at contact, which lifts the shot. In lab tests, higher balls needed more thigh turn-in and hip tilt. Failed high volleys had less hip turn-in and a more downward leg swing.
common_mistakes.fix: Let it drop below the knee, or turn side-on, lean away and swing flat.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head up early to see the goal
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The head lifts and the shoulders open, so the body tips back. The 9 ms touch is too short to steer with your eyes. A still head keeps the body over the ball. In penalties, scored kicks had a longer steady look at the ball (45% vs 18% of the run-up).
common_mistakes.fix: Keep your head still and watch the ball onto the laces. Look up after the kicking foot lands.

drills: Hover spotting (no kick, solo): drop the ball from waist height on turf and catch it at the top of its bounce, about 30-42 cm up. This teaches where the ball hangs still. 10 catches.

Wall half-volley (solo): stand 2-3 m from a solid wall. Drop the ball, and as it bounces up, half-volley it softly into the wall with toes down. Aim at a tape line at knee height. 10 per foot, then step back 1 m at a time (We Make Footballers).
Top-of-bounce volley (solo): same as above, but strike at the top of the bounce. It is the easiest timing window.
Full volley from the hands (solo): drop from waist height and volley it before it lands, into the wall below the tape line. Use half power and check that the ball comes back low.
Keep-it-down count (solo): drop, bounce and volley 5 times in a row that hit the wall under knee height. Then 10 in a row.
Partner hand-serve (pair): the partner stands 5 m away and gives underarm throws. Volley the ball back into their hands at chest height or lower. Swap after 10. Focus on 'nose over knee', not power.

Throw-bounce-volley at goal (pair): throw the ball up, let it bounce and volley at goal from about 12-18 m, adjusted for age (Soccer Coach Weekly). Progress: no bounce, then serves from left and right.
Side-on volley (pair): the partner throws a waist-high ball from the side. Lean away, pivot on the standing foot, swing flat and hit the top half into a low target (Soccer Coach Weekly).

Safety for all drills: clear the area, and make sure nobody stands behind or next to the wall or target. Warm up first and start at half power. Use a correctly pumped ball of the right size for your age. Practise jumping or scissor volleys only on soft grass with a coach.
animation_ideas: The thin goal: point of view from the edge of the box. A cone from ball to goal is only about 8 degrees tall. A hand with a fist at arm's length covers it. Then tilt the cone up 5 degrees and show the ball 1.4 m over the bar.

Laces as a racket face: side view of the shin and foot as a tennis racket. The knee rolls over the ball and the face closes (ball path goes low). The body leans back and the face opens (ball path climbs). Label: 'tilt 5 degrees = 1.4 m higher at 16 m'.

Race against the drop: a timeline bar for the 70 ms final whip. Next to it, the ball falls 30-40 cm in the same time. Put a green band (top half of ball) and a red band (bottom half) on the ball. Show where the laces land if the foot is early or late.

Raindrop vs bubble: two stopwatches. A falling ball crosses 1 cm in about 2 thousandths of a second. A ball at the top of its bounce stays in that 1 cm for about 90 thousandths of a second. A 'hover meter' fills up for the second ball.
Free topspin: slow-motion x-ray of the 9 ms touch. The falling ball slides down the laces, sticks and rolls forward over the top. Curved forward-spin arrows appear.
Spin push arrows: a flying ball with a constant 'Earth's pull' arrow and a 'spin push' arrow of about half its size. Air streams flick up off the back of the ball. Label: '90 km/h, 4 turns a second'.
Ghost paths from 16 m: three balls leave at the same angle. Backspin floats over the bar. No spin grazes the bar. Topspin dives about 1.3 m lower and goes under.
Harder is higher: two balls at the same take-off angle, 72 km/h and 90 km/h. The slower ball dips under the bar. The faster ball clears it. Caption: 'less time to fall'.
Closing speed bars: three cases side by side. Ball coming at you (adds about a fifth to two fifths of its speed), ball falling (adds almost nothing), ball moving away (takes some away).
Pendulum vs door: top view of a side-on swing (a door: timing errors go left or right) next to a side view of a front-on swing (a pendulum: timing errors go up or down).

Head-lock camera: a camera fixed to the player's head. The ball stays in the centre of the frame as the head turns with it. A 9 ms flash at contact, captioned 'too quick to steer, so keep the head still'.
Match data dots: 507 dots for non-penalty goals, with 96 lit up for volleys and half-volleys. Then two bars: about half of volleys miss the target, against about a third of normal shots.
Skid on: a topspin volley bounces in front of the keeper and keeps about 75% of its forward speed. A speed bar barely drops, and the keeper's dive arrives late.
research.chip_mirror:
CHIP MIRROR, about 26 s. Split screen, same ball and same air, one flipped arrow. Blue = chip (backspin), orange = volley (topspin).

0-4 s. Left: the foot stabs low under the ball, about 2-4 cm above the grass, and the ball rolls backward (blue arrows). Right: knee over the ball, laces on the top half, and the ball rolls forward (orange arrows). VO: "Same ball. Same air. Opposite spin."

4-10 s. Air streams. Left: the air flicks down off the back, and an arrow points up, labelled "float". The push is about a quarter of the ball's weight at about 50 km/h with 6 turns a second (verified model). Right: the air flicks up off the back, and an arrow points down, labelled "dive". The push is about half the ball's weight at 90 km/h with 4 turns a second (new model, assumed spin). VO: "Roll it backward and the air holds it up. Roll it forward and the air shoves it down, on top of Earth's pull."

10-17 s. Flight paths. Left: a slow, high arc at about 45-55 km/h hangs about 2 seconds and floats over a rushing keeper. A dotted no-spin ghost flies a little lower and lands sooner. Right: a fast arc reaches a goal 16 m away in about 0.7 s and dives under the bar. A dotted no-spin ghost clears the bar. VO: "The chip floats over the keeper. The volley dives under the bar."

17-23 s. Landing. Left: the ball lands, a backward skid arrow flashes, and a speed bar drops to about 4 in 10 (38%): "brakes". Right: the ball lands and the bar stays near 3 in 4 (75%): "skids on". VO: "When they land, the chip sits down. The volley skids on at the keeper." On-screen note: lab mat, real grass differs.

23-26 s. Both halves merge into one ball with a spin dial. Turn it back: float and brake. Turn it forward: dive and run. VO: "Get under it to make it float. Get over it to make it dive."

Accuracy rules: real kicks spin at no more than about 10 turns a second, so keep spin arrows modest. Backspin holds the ball up but also brakes it, because spin adds air drag. Say 'about' for every number.
misconceptions: 'Watch the ball hit your foot so you can steer it.' The touch lasts about 9 ms, far too short to react to. Even in cricket, what the eye sees at contact is not needed to make contact. Watching it onto the foot helps because it keeps the head still and the body over the ball.

'Hit it harder to keep it down.' It is the opposite. A faster ball has less time to fall, so the same take-off angle flies higher at the goal. Keep it down with the laces face and contact point, not with power.

'A volley always uses the ball's pace.' Only the part of the ball's speed that comes straight at the foot helps, and only about a fifth to two fifths of it carries into the shot. A ball that drops straight down adds almost no speed. It mainly changes the direction and adds forward spin.

'In a half-volley the ball is nearly still.' Just after the bounce the ball rises at its fastest. But it rises slower than it fell, because turf takes about 35-45% of its speed. The bounce also fixes the spot and the height. The nearly-still moment is the top of the bounce, which is the easiest volley of all.

'Topspin makes the shot faster.' Spin does not add flight speed. It bends the path down, so a higher take-off angle still comes in under the bar. After a bounce, a topspin ball keeps much more forward speed (about 75%) than a backspin ball (about 38%).

'Topspin makes the target bigger.' In the model, topspin shifts the working take-off angles about 5 degrees higher, but the window stays about 8 degrees wide. It forgives a slightly high strike, not a bad one.
'Leaning back gives more power.' Power comes from the hip turn and the whip of the leg. Leaning back mostly opens the laces face and lifts the ball.
'The follow-through steers the ball.' The ball leaves after about 9 ms. A good follow-through only shows that the foot was still speeding up at contact.

'Great strikers hit the middle of the ball for power.' From side to side, yes. Up and down, the fastest contact in models is 2-4 cm below the middle, but that also lifts the ball. Volleys trade a little speed for a lower path by hitting on or just above the middle.

verdicts.claim: Definitions: volley struck first-time as the ball drops out of the air; hit on the bounce = half-volley; 'a highly technical finish'.
verdicts.note: Exact wording: 'A volley is when a player strikes the ball first-time as it's dropping out of the air. If it bounces before the player connects with it, or they hit it on the bounce, it's classed as a half volley.' The page also says 'a highly technical finish'.

verdicts.claim: US Youth Soccer: 'introduce half volley & volley shooting' at U12, 'half volley & volley shooting' at U14.
verdicts.note: Both phrases are in the curriculum list (U12 and U14). The word 'develop' is not in the text. It is a fair label only.

verdicts.claim: USYS half-volley instep cues: plant foot alongside as it bounces, head and knee over it, hit no more than 2 in off the ground, toes down and curled back, raise the knee on the follow-through.
verdicts.note: All cues are verbatim under 'Shooting - half volley, Forward Instep Drive'. The page also says 'strike the ball through the point where lines A and B cross' (the centre) and 'the follow through is most important for power'. 2 in = 5.1 cm.

verdicts.claim: USYS volley instep cues: ball below knee height, hip and knee over it, hit at or slightly above line A to keep it low, toes down, ankle locked, watch the foot connect, look up after the foot is down. Shorter backswing than for a ground ball.
verdicts.corrected_value: All cues confirmed, except the 'shorter backswing' comes from the volley PASSING section. The volley SHOOTING cue says 'the kicking leg is lifted back and up so that it can swing down and through to give the required power'.
verdicts.note: The shooting section also says 'hit the ball low (at and slightly below line A) if height is required'. Do not say that the manual gives a short backswing for volley shots.

verdicts.claim: USYS side volley: torso bent sideways over the support leg 'almost horizontal', knee well up to direct the ball down, strike at or above line A, 'the greater the extent of the turn on the standing (axis) leg the more power'. Ball struck above line A 'will be propelled downward'.
verdicts.note: All phrases are verbatim (p. 12 for line A, p. 44 for the side volley). The full sentence ends '...the more power there will be in the shot'.

verdicts.claim: Soccer Coach Weekly side-on cues: 'Upper body falls away from ball', 'Knee moves through ahead of the ball', 'Contact ball above horizontal midline', 'Body rotates around non-kicking leg', leg 'almost parallel with the ground'.
verdicts.note: All five cues are on the page. The page also says 'Extend ankle' and 'Use instep or laces'.

verdicts.claim: Volley drill cues: head and knee over the ball, lock ankle/toes down/laces, let the ball fall as low as possible, strike middle to bottom half but not underneath. Throw, bounce and volley from about 20 yards.
verdicts.note: All quotes and the setup are exact: players 'throw the ball in the air towards the goal, let it bounce then volley', from 'about 20 yards' (18.3 m), 'vary the distance depending on age and ability'. Caution: 'middle to bottom half' conflicts with the USYS and side-on cues (at or above the middle). Sugi 2020 also found that failed volleys hit the bottom part of the ball. Do not narrate the 'bottom half' cue.

verdicts.claim: Failed volleys (over the goal): 10 university players, 500 Hz; bottom-of-ball contact, less hip internal rotation in backswing, more upright foot, more downward leg swing; patterns differed between players.
verdicts.note: Sugi, Nunome, Tamura and Ismail, ISBS 2020. The abstract states all of this word for word, including 'several patterns of failed trials depending on the subjects'.

verdicts.claim: Volleys at 0/25/50/75 cm (15 players, 500 Hz): upward foot speed from knee flexion, hip internal rotation, pelvic roll and hip flexion; turn-in and hip tilt grow with ball height.
verdicts.note: Sugi et al., Sports Biomech 2022 21(6):669-684. Correct. Also, the knee-flexion and hip-flexion shares get smaller as the ball gets higher. Caveat: the ball was PLACED at each height (a stationary ball), not a falling ball.

verdicts.claim: Rolling vs stationary ball (9 skilled players): no significant difference in foot speed at contact or leg kinematics.
verdicts.note: Barnes, Sterzing and Ball (ISBS). The quote matches. The balls rolled across the kick line at 30 and 90 deg, plus a dribble condition, recorded at 250 Hz. The ball was not a ball in the air or a ball coming at the kicker.

verdicts.claim: Moving-ball kicks (8 experienced, 10 less experienced): no peak foot-speed difference; experienced more accurate; time from peak hip angle to contact longer for a moving ball.
verdicts.note: Egan, Verheul and Savelsbergh 2007, J Mot Behav 39:423-432. The abstract confirms n, equal foot speed and better accuracy. It also reports a smaller knee range of motion for the moving ball. The hip-angle timing is not in the abstract. A thesis that summarises the paper states it (diva-portal FULLTEXT04, p. 8).

verdicts.claim: Machine-served volleys at 9.0/11.5/15.0 m/s (9 players): ball speed tracked foot speed in every condition; ball/foot ratio highest when the ball met the middle of the foot.
verdicts.note: Tani, Kidokoro and Yanai 2013, JSME Symposium on Sports and Human Dynamics. CiNii marks it 'reviewed: false' (conference paper). 'Middle of the foot' means across its width (near the foot's mid-sagittal plane), not along its length. 32-54 km/h is correct.

verdicts.claim: Instep kick timing (20 elite players): backswing 0.112 s, leg cocking 0.072 s, max knee flexion to impact 0.070 +/- 0.007 s, whole kick 0.603 s.
verdicts.note: Langhout et al. 2015 values, as tabulated in the review. The acceleration phase is defined as MKF to ball impact. The 0.603 s runs from toe-off to the end of the follow-through. Toe-off to impact is 0.45 s. These are maximal kicks at a STATIONARY ball, not volleys.

verdicts.claim: OWN CALC: ball dropped from 1.5-2 m reaches 0.4 m at 4.7-5.6 m/s; falls 30-37 cm in the last 70 ms, 56-70 cm in the last 142 ms; 1 cm per 1.8-2.2 ms.
verdicts.note: My re-calculation gives 4.65-5.60 m/s (16.7-20.2 km/h), 30.2-36.8 cm, 56-70 cm and 1.79-2.15 ms per cm. Drag is less than 4% of weight at these speeds. Caveat: this is a self-dropped ball. A ball that drops from a cross or lob with a 5-8 m peak reaches knee height at about 10-12 m/s, so it moves 1 cm in about 1 ms.

verdicts.claim: OWN CALC: at the top of a bounce the ball stays <1 cm from its peak for ~90 ms, <2 cm for ~130 ms; ~25x more forgiving than a ball falling at 20 km/h.
verdicts.corrected_value: 90 ms and 128 ms are correct. The 25x holds only for the same +/-1 cm tolerance: about 90 ms at the peak vs about 3.6 ms for a ball falling at 20 km/h.
verdicts.note: If the viewer compares '90 ms' with '1 cm in about 2 ms' (as in steps 4 and 9), they get about 45-50x. Compare like with like on screen. Also, USYS teaches hitting the half-volley just off the ground (2 in or less), where the ball rises fastest, not at the top of the bounce.

verdicts.claim: FIFA turf: 2 m drop rebounds 0.60-0.85 m; leaves at 55-65% of landing speed; 1 m drop bounces 30-42 cm and rises at 2.4-2.9 m/s.
verdicts.corrected_value: Arithmetic correct (sqrt 0.30-0.425 = 0.55-0.65; 2.43-2.89 m/s). But the 35-45% speed loss is ball plus turf, not turf alone.
verdicts.note: A FIFA ball on steel already rebounds only 135-155 cm from 2 m, so it loses about 12-18% of its speed with no turf. This is a lab drop test on artificial turf. Natural grass varies. At a lower drop height the rebound share can be a little higher.

verdicts.claim: Contact ~10 mm below centre for a high target, near centre for a low target (7 players, 42 trials).
verdicts.note: Inoue, Smith and Nunome, ISBS 2025, 2000 Hz. The same abstract says the instep faced more downward for the low target. This supports the 'close the face' idea. The ball was on the ground, not a volley.

verdicts.claim: FE model: fastest ball from contact 2-4 cm below centre; max take-off 16 deg at 2 cm below (Asai 2005, in Lees review).
verdicts.note: Verified earlier and still valid. This is a simulation.

verdicts.claim: OWN MODEL (contact 0.4 m, goal 16 m): take-off angles under a 2.44 m bar span ~8 deg (~7 deg for 2.13 m). 1 deg = 28 cm at 16 m, 5 deg = 1.4 m.
verdicts.note: My run (ball centre 0.11-2.33 m at the line, C_D 0-0.3) gives 7.9-8.5 deg. A straight line for the youth bar gives 6.8 deg. 16 tan1 = 0.279 m and 16 tan5 = 1.40 m. Caveat: the window counts only shots that reach the line in the air. A low shot that bounces first can still score.

verdicts.claim: OWN MODEL no spin from 16 m: window ~12-21 deg at 72 km/h, ~7-15 deg at 90 km/h; harder hit flies higher at the line (0.7 s vs 0.9 s).
verdicts.note: My point-mass run with C_D 0.15-0.3 gives 11.6-12.9 to 19.9-21.4 deg at 20 m/s and 6.9-7.7 to 14.9-15.8 deg at 25 m/s. Flight times are 0.87-0.93 s and 0.70-0.75 s. This holds at a FIXED take-off angle.

verdicts.claim: OWN MODEL: 4 rev/s topspin at 90 km/h arrives ~1.25-1.3 m lower at 16 m (~1.6 m at 72 km/h); window shifts up ~5 deg, not wider.
verdicts.corrected_value: About 0.7-1.3 m lower at 90 km/h and about 0.9-1.6 m at 72 km/h. The window shifts about 2.5-5 deg and stays about 8 deg wide.
verdicts.note: The result depends on C_L at Sp 0.11-0.14. Asai 2007 measured C_S of only about 0.1 at Sp 0.1, which gives about 0.7-0.8 m and a 2.5-3 deg shift. A linear fit through C_S 0.25 at Sp 0.18 gives C_L of about 0.15, which gives about 1.0-1.2 m. The claimed 1.25-1.3 m needs C_L of about 0.175-0.2. The 'no wider' result holds in every case. The spin rate is still an assumption.

verdicts.claim: Asai 2007 C_S ~0.25 at 27 m/s and 7 rev/s gives ~4.1 N (about the 4.2 N weight). At 25 m/s and 4 rev/s the model gives ~2.5 N, half to two thirds of the weight.
verdicts.corrected_value: 4.1-4.2 N confirmed. At 25 m/s and 4 rev/s: about 1.4-2.5 N, about one third to one half of the weight.
verdicts.note: 0.5 x 1.2 x 27^2 x 0.038 x 0.25 = 4.16 N. Asai 2007 states that 'When the Sp was 0.1, the Cs decreased to 0.1'. At Sp 0.11 that gives 1.4 N (0.34 W). 2.5 N needs C_L 0.175, which is above the measured value.

verdicts.claim: Launcher tests used pure backspin or pure topspin; lift along spin x velocity so topspin pushes down; C_L ~0.35 at Sp 0.5 and 14 m/s.
verdicts.note: Goff and Carre 2012: 'we examined either pure backspin or pure topspin'. Lift 'usually points in the direction of omega x v'. C_L is about 0.35 at v about 14 m/s and Sp about 0.5. Launch speeds stayed under 20 m/s. For Sp < 0.3 they matched the wind-tunnel data.

verdicts.claim: Bush: Folha Seca struck with nearly pure topspin, 'dips dramatically'; 'While volleying a ball with topspin is relatively straightforward, imparting pure topspin is extremely difficult to do from a dead ball.'
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the chapter. The sentence continues '...and only a few players have truely mastered it.'

verdicts.claim: OWN RIGID-BALL ESTIMATE: falling ball on a level foot slides, grips, keeps ~60% of fall speed downward, leaves 5-10 deg below the push line with ~3.5-5 rev/s topspin; a foot rising faster than the ball falls gives backspin.
verdicts.note: My hollow-sphere (k = 2/3) rolling-at-release model gives the same: 60% of the fall speed kept, 3.5-4.9 rev/s for 4-5.6 m/s, 5-10 deg below the push line for foot speeds of 15-20 m/s. Grip needs friction of only about 0.08. The spin direction (topspin) is correct. Cross shows slide-then-grip for tennis balls on strings, but also a late release with backward slip. So the real spin can differ. No volley spin has been measured. Keep the confidence low.

verdicts.claim: OWN CALC: shot speed = (1.17-1.39) x foot speed + (0.17-0.39) x oncoming speed (M 1.7-2.1 kg, e 0.46-0.68); 10 m/s oncoming adds 2-4 m/s; a dropping ball adds almost nothing (closing speed 20.8 m/s).
verdicts.note: The 1-D collision formula checks: M(1+e)/(M+m) = 1.165-1.394, and (eM-m)/(M+m) = 0.165-0.394. sqrt(20^2+5.6^2) = 20.8. Caveats: M comes from an Australian-football kicking machine, and e falls at higher impact speeds. For youth (ball/foot ratio about 1.0-1.2) the oncoming share is nearer 10%.

verdicts.claim: Earlier verified: contact ~9 ms; locked ankle ~4% faster in a machine; fastest spot mid-laces ~6 cm in front of the ankle, toe/ankle ~15% slower; shank still speeding up at impact; plant foot behind makes the ball rise.
verdicts.note: All are in the earlier verification. All come from stationary-ball instep kicks. The 4% came from an Australian-football machine.

verdicts.claim: Kellis and Katis: 'Accurate kicks are generally slower than powerful kicks.' Max instep ball speed 18-35 m/s.
verdicts.note: Both are verbatim in the JSSM 2007 review.

verdicts.claim: Youth shot speeds ~67/77/81 km/h at U13/U15/U17; ball/foot ratio ~1.0 (U9) to 1.26 (U20).
verdicts.note: Verified earlier (Vieira et al. Table 1).

verdicts.claim: Bahill and LaRitz 1984: major-league batter tracked to ~5.5 ft, eye speed up to 120 deg/s; others lost it ~9 ft; one batter jumped his eyes ahead.
verdicts.note: The SABR article quotes all of these: 'tracked the ball accurately until about 5.5 feet', 'as high as 120 degrees per second', 'about 9 feet away', and a 'predictive or anticipatory saccade'. This is baseball with a very small sample.

verdicts.claim: Mann et al. 2013: elite head-ball angle 2.4 +/- 1.7 deg (club 3.7); gaze on contact spot 80-100% of trials; 'ball could be followed if the batters simply moved their head and kept their eyes still'; contact information 'not necessary to make contact'.
verdicts.note: All values and both quotes are exact. Sample: only 2 elite and 2 club batters. Important: the elite batters did NOT keep their eyes still. They made two predictive saccades, to the bounce and to the bat-ball contact spot. Their HEAD turned with the ball.

verdicts.claim: Land and McLeod 2000: saccade to the bounce point, follow for 100-200 ms after the bounce; a faster first eye jump went with better batting.
verdicts.corrected_value: A SHORT LATENCY (an earlier start) of the first saccade distinguished good from poor batsmen. The study did not report a faster saccade.
verdicts.note: The abstract says the eyes 'make a predictive saccade to the place where they expect it to hit the ground, wait for it to bounce, and follow its trajectory for 100-200 ms after the bounce'. It compared only a few batsmen.

verdicts.claim: Quiet eye: final steady look >=100 ms within 3 deg (Vickers); in penalties longer in scored (45 +/- 29%) than missed (18 +/- 10%) kicks.
verdicts.corrected_value: Numbers correct. They are QE as a percentage of trial time, from 12 university players (one scored and one missed penalty each), in an indoor lab.
verdicts.note: Timmis, Piras and van Paridon 2018. This paper sets the QE offset at gaze leaving the ball by 1 deg for more than 100 ms. The 3 deg / 100 ms definition is Vickers' general one (see Vickers et al. 2019). The ball was stationary, so this says nothing about volleys.

verdicts.claim: People intercept fast targets with very high timing precision and adjust where rather than when they hit, if given the choice. ~5-6 ms from a search summary only.
verdicts.note: Brenner and Smeets 2015 abstract: temporal precision 'was highest for fast targets that subjects were free to intercept wherever they wished' and 'people adjusted where rather than when they would hit the target if given the choice'. I could not open the full text (403). The 5-6 ms figure is still UNVERIFIABLE. Do not narrate it. The targets were virtual and intercepted by hand.

verdicts.claim: StatsBomb 230 matches: volleys 36 and half-volleys 60 of 507 NP goals (19%); conversion volleys 10.3% (350), half-volleys 8.8% (685), normal foot ~8.4%.
verdicts.note: I replicated this from the raw open data: 230 matches, 507 non-penalty goals (shoot-outs excluded), Volley 36/350 = 10.3%, Half Volley 60/685 = 8.8%, Normal foot shots 286/3434 = 8.3%. These are raw rates that do not adjust for chance quality. Volleys came from closer.

verdicts.claim: StatsBomb: 54% of volleys, 45% of half-volleys missed target vs 34% of normal foot shots; 21.5% of volleys over the bar vs 17.2%; median 14.3 m vs 20.2 m.
verdicts.note: Replicated: 53.7%, 44.8% and 33.5% (Off T + Wayward + Post). Over the bar (end z > 2.67 yd): volleys 21.5%, normal foot 17.2%. Half-volleys ALSO went over 21.5%. Some misses lack an end height, so the over-bar rates are lower bounds. The median distances are 14.3 m and 20.2 m (half-volleys 15.6 m).

verdicts.claim: PL 2008/09: 69.3% of goals zero-possession; 132 Puskas nominees 2009-2021: 56.1% airborne; 51.5% facing, 31.8% side, 16.7% back; side volley reach ~0.4 body heights per leg.
verdicts.note: All values are in Shan and Zhang 2022 (Bioengineering 9:333). The 69.3% is cited from Durlik and Bieniek 2014. It counts all one-touch shots (headers included), not volleys only. Puskas nominees are a biased set of spectacular goals. The 0.4 BH is a model input taken from other studies.

verdicts.claim: Solo wall drill: stand a few feet from a wall, drop, volley as it bounces up, move back and aim at spots; keep head and knee over the ball, avoid leaning back.
verdicts.note: Quotes confirmed: 'get both your head and knee over the ball as well as ensuring that you are not leaning back'. The page says to move 'further and further away'. I did not see 'aim at spots on the wall'. The same page also says 'the power and the direction come from the follow through', which misconception 8 contradicts.

verdicts.claim: Bounce test (rubber mat): backspin kept ~38% of forward speed, topspin ~75%.
verdicts.note: Verified earlier (Rezaei 2011). Caveats: a rubber mat, 18-19 m/s impacts at 23-30 deg, and unmatched angles. This was not a dipping volley landing on grass.

mechanism_errors: Step 1 (eye claims): no eye-tracking study of soccer volleys exists in these sources. 'Look ahead, then turn the head with it' comes from cricket (Land & McLeod; Mann et al. used only 2 elite and 2 club batters) and baseball. Say 'In cricket, top batters...' or 'probably'. The predictive jump to the bounce spot fits a half-volley better than a dropping volley.

Step 1 and claim 14: '20 km/h near knee height' holds only for a ball dropped from about 1.5-2 m. A cross or lob falling from a 5-8 m peak reaches knee height at about 35-45 km/h. It then moves 1 cm in about 1 ms, not 2 ms.
Step 3: the 70 ms final whip comes from maximal kicks at a STATIONARY ball by elite adults (Langhout 2015). No one has measured volley timing. Say 'in a full-power kick'.

Step 5: '5 degrees of tilt puts the ball 1.4 m higher' treats face tilt as launch angle. The ball leaves between the face normal and the foot path. For a ball that grips, the launch angle changes by only about 0.7 times the face tilt, so 5 deg of tilt gives about 3.5 deg, or about 1 m at 16 m. The 1.4 m is right only for a 5 deg change in LAUNCH angle. An open face also adds backspin lift, so 'about a metre or more' is safe.

Steps 5 and 6, chip mirror 'laces on the top half': from knee height, a ball that leaves flat or downward at 90 km/h hits the grass about 5-7 m out. To reach a goal 16 m away in the air, the model needs about 7-15 deg UP with no spin, or about 10-20 deg up with topspin. 'Close the face' means 'do not launch too steeply', not 'launch down'. Animate the ball leaving at about 10-20 deg up.

Step 6: 'Forward spin comes almost for free' holds only when the foot moves level or downward relative to the falling ball. Volley foot paths often have an upward speed (Sugi et al. 2022 studied what makes it). If the foot rises as fast as the ball falls, there is no spin. If it rises faster, the ball gets backspin. No volley spin rate has been measured. Say 'can come almost for free'.

Step 7: 'about half the ball's weight' and '1.3 m lower' are at the top of the plausible range. Asai 2007 measured C_S of only about 0.1 at Sp 0.1, which gives about a third of the weight and about 0.7-0.8 m of extra dip. Say 'a third to a half of its weight' and 'up to about a metre lower'. The window shift is about 2.5-5 deg, not a flat 5 deg.

Step 9: 'Certified turf takes 35-45% of the ball's speed' is wrong about the cause. That loss is ball PLUS turf in a drop test on artificial turf. The ball alone on steel already loses about 12-18%. Say 'the bounce takes about 35-45% of its speed'. Also, striking at the top of the bounce is not the USYS half-volley (hit 2 in or less off the ground, when the ball rises fastest). Match data do not show that half-volleys are easier either: in StatsBomb data they went over the bar as often as volleys (21.5%). They missed the target less (45% vs 54%).

Step 10 and chip mirror 'skids on': 'skid' means to slide without rolling, which is what a BACKSPIN ball does. A topspin ball keeps its pace because its surface slips less on the ground. Say 'runs on' or 'keeps its pace', as the mirror's own ending does ('dive and run'). Keep the 'lab mat' note: the 75% came from 18-19 m/s shallow impacts on rubber.

Misconception 1: 'helps because it keeps the head still' contradicts step 1 and the cricket data. Elite batters TURNED the head with the ball (head-ball angle about 2.4 deg) and jumped the eyes AHEAD to the contact spot. They did this in 80-100% of trials. Better: 'Looking at the contact spot may help by keeping the head down and over the ball. That is a coaching idea, not a tested result.' The 9 ms and 'not needed to make contact' points are correct.
Misconception 3: the 'a fifth to two fifths' share is for skilled adults. For youth players (ball/foot ratio about 1.0-1.2), only about a tenth of the oncoming speed carries into the shot.

Misconception 4: 'the top of the bounce is the easiest volley of all' has no source. The timing slack is real (about 25x for a +/-1 cm target), but no study shows that the strike is easier or scores more. 'Turf takes 35-45%' must say ball and turf together.
Misconception 6: the shift is about 2.5-5 deg (depends on the unmeasured spin and C_L), not 'about 5 degrees'. 'The window stays about 8 degrees wide' is correct.

Misconception 8: 'A good follow-through only shows that the foot was still speeding up' is too narrow. It also shows the swing direction at contact. USYS uses a knee raise on the follow-through to keep the ball under the bar.

Chip mirror, 4-10 s: the volley push 'about half the ball's weight' must be 'about a third to a half' (assumed 4 rev/s). The chip value (about a quarter at 50 km/h and 6 rev/s) is correct. Also note that the chip flies in the high-drag regime (at or below the drag crisis), while the 90 km/h volley is above it. 'Same air' is fine, but the drag differs a lot.
safe_numbers_for_narration: A volley is struck first time as the ball drops out of the air. Hit it on the bounce and it is a half-volley (England Football).
US Youth Soccer introduces half-volley and volley shooting at U12. It teaches hitting the half-volley no more than about 5 cm (2 in) off the ground.
In a study of 10 university players, failed volleys that flew over the goal hit the bottom part of the ball with a more upright foot (Sugi et al. 2020).
Kicking a moving ball did not change top foot speed, and experienced players were more accurate (8 experienced vs 10 less experienced players).
In machine-served volleys at about 32-54 km/h, ball speed went up with foot speed in every condition (9 players, conference paper).
In a full-power kick at a still ball, the last whip of the leg, from full knee bend to impact, takes about 70 thousandths of a second (20 elite players).
A ball dropped from about head height reaches knee height at about 17-20 km/h. In the last 70 ms it falls about 30-37 cm, and it moves 1 cm in about 2 ms.
At the top of a bounce, the ball stays within 1 cm of its highest point for about 90 ms, and within 2 cm for about 130 ms.
For the same plus-or-minus 1 cm target, the top of a bounce gives about 25 times more timing slack than a ball falling at 20 km/h (about 90 ms vs about 4 ms).
On FIFA-tested artificial turf, a ball dropped from 2 m bounces back only about 0.60-0.85 m. It leaves at about 55-65% of its landing speed (ball and turf together).
From 16 m, with contact at knee height, the goal spans only about 8 degrees of take-off angle. One degree moves the ball about 28 cm at the goal.
With no spin from 16 m, the take-off angles that score are about 12-21 degrees at 72 km/h but about 7-15 degrees at 90 km/h (model).
From 16 m, the ball takes about 0.9 s at 72 km/h and about 0.7 s at 90 km/h, so a harder hit has less time to fall.
With an assumed 4 turns a second of topspin at 90 km/h, the ball arrives up to about 1 m lower than a no-spin shot, and the scoring window shifts about 3-5 degrees without getting wider (model).
At 90 km/h and 4 turns a second, the topspin push is about a third to a half of the ball's weight (model, assumed spin).
At 97 km/h and 7 turns a second, the spin force is about 4 N, about the ball's own weight (Asai 2007 wind tunnel).
A chip at about 50 km/h with 6 turns a second of backspin gets about a quarter of its weight in lift (model with measured coefficients).
For a skilled adult, only about a fifth to two fifths of an oncoming ball's speed carries into the shot. A 36 km/h oncoming ball adds only about 7-14 km/h (collision model).
Foot and ball touch for only about 9 thousandths of a second in a hard instep kick.
The fastest contact spot is the middle of the laces, about 6 cm in front of the ankle. Toe or ankle contact gave about 15% less speed.
'Accurate kicks are generally slower than powerful kicks' (Kellis and Katis review).
Youth shot speeds: about 67 km/h at U13, 77 km/h at U15, 81 km/h at U17.
A major-league batter followed the pitch with his eyes until it was about 1.7 m away, with eye speeds up to about 120 degrees a second. Other batters lost it at about 2.7 m.
Two elite cricket batters kept their head pointed within about 2.4 degrees of the ball, and jumped their eyes ahead to the bat-ball contact spot in 80-100% of trials.
Cricket batsmen jump their eyes to where the ball will bounce, then follow it for about 100-200 ms after the bounce. An earlier first eye jump went with better batting.
In one small penalty study (12 university players), the final steady look at the ball took about 45% of the time in scored kicks vs about 18% in missed kicks.
At the 2018 and 2022 World Cups and Euro 2020 and 2024, about 1 in 5 non-penalty goals (96 of 507) came from volleys or half-volleys (StatsBomb open data).
In the same data, volleys scored about 10% of the time, half-volleys about 9% and normal foot shots about 8%. Volleys were taken from closer, a median of about 14 m vs 20 m.
In the same data, about 54% of volleys missed the target vs about 34% of normal foot shots. About 1 in 5 volleys went over the bar.
Of 132 FIFA Puskas Award nominated goals (2009-2021), about 56% were struck from a ball in the air.
In one lab bounce test on a rubber mat, a ball with backspin kept only about 38% of its forward speed. A ball with topspin kept about 75%.
Real kicks spin at no more than about 10 turns a second (Asai 2007).
MIT's John Bush: 'While volleying a ball with topspin is relatively straightforward, imparting pure topspin is extremely difficult to do from a dead ball.'

result.scores:
SCORES (1-10). Criteria in order: hook / clarity for a 12-year-old / zero jargon / physics accuracy / practical value / visual variety and SVG feasibility / pacing / length.

DRAFT A 'Three Spins and a Line': 9 / 8 / 9 / 7 / 8 / 9 / 9 / 8 = 67 of 80.
- Hook 9: a miss every player knows, a made-up keeper, a planted motif and a clear question.
- Clarity 8: short plain lines. 'Fingertips, not net.' and 'Frisbee in the wind.' are hard to decode.
- Jargon 9: clean, except one 'Backspin'.
- Physics 7: the numbers come from the lists. But 'Your toes? Car speed, about eighty' gives an adult number as the viewer's own (U13 shots average about 67 km/h). 'Keepers are bad at reading sideways drift' stretches a novice VR result. 'Often almost free' has no data for 'often'.
- Practical 8: each chapter has a cue, a mistake, a fix and a drill. But the curler has no ankle cue, and only one drill shows safety.
- Visual 9: one world. The spin line is drawn from the real spin state. The keeper is an all-white rig that is cheap to draw. But the kit has 23 components.
- Pacing 9. Length 8: 923 words but about 6:37. The knuckle teaser runs 28 s.

DRAFT B 'Three Kinds of Spin': 8 / 8 / 8 / 9 / 9 / 8 / 9 / 8 = 67 of 80.
- Hook 8: a bold 'you' claim and a funny shouting line, but no story or stakes.
- Clarity 8: strong metaphors (squashy gear, soap bubble, car park). 'Two thousandths of a second' and 'penalties aside' are heavy.
- Jargon 8: 'particles' and 'gravity' are mild science words.
- Physics 9: correct qualifiers ('in a skilled adult's kick', 'when your foot swings level', 'the keeper has almost no time').
- Practical 9: one PracticeBoard layout per chapter, a safety line on every drill, and the toes-up curler cue.
- Visual 8: good scale shifts and a dot grid. But the metaphor grab bag has 15 kinds, 400 particles have faces, and the kit has 24 components.
- Pacing 9. Length 8: 931 words, about 6:34. Chapter 3 runs 104 s, plus a 32 s practice block.

FLIGHT CHECK: I re-ran every flight in both drafts with a point-mass model (air brake plus spin push). All stated heights and times match in 0.05 m and 0.02 s. The flights are not the problem.

VERDICT: a tie on points. A wins on the brief's narrative spine. The miss becomes an accidental chip, Chalk sets one problem per chapter, and the line shows the spin in every shot. B's strengths are fixes and single lines that graft cleanly.

GRAFTED FROM B: 'After that, it's on its own' and the shouting gag (pays off as 'No shouting needed'). 'In a skilled adult's kick'. The toes-up, ankle-locked curler cue. The squashy gear. The Air Crowd as a small character. 'So the keeper sees it late'. The one-in-five volley goal stat with the 507-dot grid. 'Hold your fist at arm's length'. 'Swing level' as the condition for free forward spin. 'Harder means higher'. The soap bubble. 'Hello, car park' (set up by a car alarm in s01). The age-ticker gag. The city-lights pull-back. One PracticeBoard with safety on every drill. B's three-note title motif and its reused practice music loop.

FIXES TO A: cut 'keepers are bad', 'often' and 'Backspin'. Changed 'Spin costs speed' to 'More spin, less speed', so spin is not named as the cause of the lost speed. Changed 'three metres outside the post' to 'outside your target'. Cut the knuckle teaser from 67 to 49 words. Changed the knuckle side force from A's 1 N to the verified 2 N peak (sine, phase 0.79 rad). This gives about 0.4 m of wander with 3 small reversals. Random flips gave up to 3.5 m of drift, so I rejected them. Merged the kit from 23 to 18 components.

FINAL: 23 scenes, 939 words, about 389 s (6:16 at a flat 150 wpm). The chip moment runs 27 s and the teaser 20 s. Each scene runs 10-24 s. No chapter has more than 2 spoken numbers.

issues.problem: The aim-at-target miss goes the wrong way. The curler comes from the left channel, aims at the far (right) corner and bends right to left. If you aim straight at the far corner, the spin pulls the ball about 2.7 m LEFT, toward the middle of the goal. It does not go past the post and wide. My run of the kit model (19 m/s, 20 deg, 7 rev/s, axis 63 deg, Cd 0.27) puts CURLER_AIM_MISS 2.73 m left of the target at 1.0 m high after 1.34 s. The research misconception says 'the spin carries the ball past it', which means past the target point, not past the post. Direction source: curler verification ('A right-footer's inside-foot curler spins anticlockwise from above and bends right to left'), Asai 2007 https://people.stfx.ca/smackenz/courses/HK474/Labs/Jump%20Float%20Lab/Asai%202007%20Fundamental%20aerodynamics%20of%20the%20soccer%20ball.pdf
issues.fix: Narration: 'Classic mistake: aiming at the target. The spin pulls it back to the middle, straight to Chalk.' Visual beats: 'A ghost ball launches straight at the far corner.' then 'It bends back toward the middle of the goal and crosses about 2.7 m inside the far post, in Chalk's reach bubble. He catches it. A drift bracket shows the 2.7 m.' physics_sim: 'CURLER_AIM_MISS: same spin, launched straight at the far corner. It crosses the line about 2.7 m to the left of the corner (toward the middle), about 1.0 m high, after about 1.34 s.'

issues.problem: The DROP sim cannot give the described path. DROP starts at rest 2.0 m up. But in the scene Chalk punches the ball 'straight up' from the goal, and then it 'falls toward Tavi', who volleys from 16 m (VOLLEY). A straight-up punch lands in the six-yard box. To go 16 m with a 2 m peak, the ball needs about 28 m/s sideways, so it is a line drive, not a drop. A real punched clearance loops from a 5-8 m peak and reaches knee height at about 35-45 km/h, not 20 km/h. The volley verification says this (mechanism_errors, step 1 and claim 14). s18 ('Chalk punches again and the ball drops') has the same fault.
issues.fix: Keep the verified self-set 2 m drop. s13 narration: 'Problem three. Chalk punches it clear. You knock it up, and it drops toward you.' s13 visual beats: 'Tavi shoots. Chalk punches the ball out to Tavi.' then 'Tavi cushions it up off his thigh to about 2 m. It falls straight down in front of him (DROP sim). Freeze mid-fall.' s18 visual beat: 'Now, for real. Chalk punches it clear again. Tavi knocks it up off his thigh, and it drops.' DROP physics_sim stays as written: at rest 2.0 m up, knee height after about 0.57 s at about 20 km/h.

issues.problem: The TOE_HIT sim cannot reach Chalk's mitten in the air. At 18.4 m/s, 9 deg up, 4 rev/s backspin and Cd 0.25, my run of the kit model hits the grass about 13.6 m out after 0.83 s. That is 4.4 m before the goal line. The height-at-the-line check in the FlightSim validator then has no value. The 15% toe loss is correct (Ishii 2012, https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/jab/28/3/article-p258.xml).
issues.fix: physics_sim: 'Inset save: TOE_HIT = 18.4 m/s (66 km/h, 15% slower than DRIVE_R), 14 deg up, 8.5 deg right, backspin 4 rev/s, Cd 0.25. It crosses about 2.7 m right of centre, about 0.35 m high, after about 1.17 s. That is about 0.2 s after DRIVE_R, so Chalk's dive with the same reaction delay reaches it. The full-speed ghost is DRIVE_R.'

issues.problem: 'The line turns like a clock hand, anticlockwise' contradicts itself. Clock hands turn clockwise. An animator who follows the clock image draws clockwise spin, and clockwise spin bends the ball left to right, the wrong way for a right-footer's inside-foot curler. The Ball character design ('clock-hand turn seen from above (curler)') has the same trap. Correct direction: anticlockwise seen from above (curler verification, Asai 2007 URL above).
issues.fix: s08 visual beat: 'You need sideways spin.' Top-view close-up of the ball. The line turns anticlockwise seen from above: its front edge swings left.' Ball design text: 'sideways turn, anticlockwise seen from above (curler)'.

issues.problem: Two problems. (1) 'on the outside half' can be heard as 'use the outside of your foot'. For a right-footer, the outside of the foot bends the ball the other way. The outside-foot Roberto Carlos kick was left-footed (https://physicsworld.com/a/the-physics-of-football/). (2) The wipe has no direction. Anticlockwise spin seen from above means the BACK of the ball moves to the right, seen from behind. So the foot must strike right of centre and drag the back of the ball to the right, toward the aim-off flag. If the wiper is drawn right to left across the back, it shows the opposite spin.
issues.fix: Narration: 'Wipe across the back, like a windscreen wiper, just right of the middle.' Visual beats: 'Wipe across the back, like a windscreen wiper,' A wiper icon sweeps forward and to the right, toward the aim-off flag, at about 45 degrees to the foot's face. It drags the back of the ball to the right.' and 'just right of the middle.' The back of the ball splits in two. The right half (seen from behind) glows green, with the contact dot on it.'

issues.problem: No scene gives the spinAxis vector. The kit uses x toward goal, y left, z up, and push along (axis x velocity). One sign error turns backspin into topspin or makes the curler bend left to right. The prose labels ('backspin', 'anticlockwise from above, part backspin') do not fix the sign. I checked the vectors below against every stated check value (MISS 3.06 m, DRIVE_R 0.42 m, CURLER 2.73 m drift, VOLLEY 1.87 m, CHIP 1.96 m). They all reproduce.
issues.fix: Add to the FlightSim notes: 'Axis vectors, for a shot a degrees right of +x (heading (cos a, -sin a, 0)): backspin = -(sin a, cos a, 0), which is [0,-1,0] for a = 0 (MISS, DRIVE_R, DRIVE_L with a mirrored, DRIVE_WALL, TOE_HIT, CHIP). Topspin = +(sin a, cos a, 0), which is [0,1,0] for a = 0 (VOLLEY). CURLER = 0.891 x [0,0,1] - 0.454 x (sin 8 deg, cos 8 deg, 0) = [-0.063, -0.450, 0.891]. The validator checks that backspin pushes up, VOLLEY pushes down and CURLER pushes toward +y (left).'

issues.problem: VOLLEY has no sideways angle. So it crosses the middle of the goal at about 1.87 m (my run: 1.875 m at 0.97 s), straight at a tall keeper standing in the middle. It cannot go 'into the top corner' or 'just past Chalk's raised mitten'. Also, the VOLLEY_GHOST lands about 23.6 m from the kick, about 7.6 m past the goal line. The car park is 12 m past the line, so the ghost cannot reach it.
issues.fix: physics_sim: 'VOLLEY: 16 m out, contact 0.4 m. 20 m/s (72 km/h), 23 deg up, 10 deg right. Forward spin 4 rev/s (assumed: no volley spin has been measured), axis (sin 10 deg, cos 10 deg, 0). Cl fixed at 0.14 (push about 1.3 N, about a third of the weight). Cd 0.27. It crosses about 2.8 m right of centre, about 1.81 m high, after about 0.99 s. VOLLEY_GHOST: same launch, no spin: about 2.78 m high, over. Gap about 0.97 m.' s16 narration: 'It dives, up to about a metre lower than with no spin. Car park, or the corner.' s16 visual: 'The ghost clears the bar and drops about 7-8 m behind the goal. Far away, the car-park hazard lights blink. The real ball drops in high, inside the right post.'

issues.problem: The landing beats do not match the sims. CHIP crosses the goal line in the air at about 1.96 m, and VOLLEY at about 1.87 m. Neither ball lands on the pitch in front of the keeper, so 'the ball lands and brakes' and 'lands and runs on' cannot come from these paths. Also, the 38% and 75% come from one rubber-mat test at 18-19 m/s and 23-30 deg with unmatched angles. They do not come from a chip or a dipping volley on grass (volley verification, Rezaei 2011, https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/1897934/2006598). The volley bar has no 'lab test' note.
issues.fix: Visual beats: 'When it lands, the chip sits down.' Both halves cut to the same strip of empty turf. The left ball lands with backward spin and brakes. Its speed bar drops to about 4 in 10. Label 'sits down'.' and 'The volley runs on.' The right ball lands with forward spin. Its bar stays near 3 in 4. Label 'runs on'. One note under both halves: 'lab test, rubber mat'.' physics_sim, add: 'The landing beats are a separate demo, not CHIP or VOLLEY. Both of those cross the goal line in the air.'

issues.problem: 'That first shot tonight? A chip.' is wrong. MISS is a 76 km/h laces drive at 18 deg, hit with a lean-back. A chip is a short stab at about 45-55 km/h that leaves at about 45 deg (chip safe list, https://chalkdustmagazine.com/blog/the-maths-behind-a-chip-goal/). The two shots share only the low contact and the backward spin. The drive research calls this a skied drive: 'your foot meets the ball on the way up and under its centre. The ball climbs and gets backspin.'
issues.fix: Narration: 'That first shot tonight? It had a chip's spin. Chest behind the ball, foot under it. Backward spin, by accident. Chip on purpose, when the keeper rushes out.' Stamp: 'CHIP SPIN, BY ACCIDENT'.

issues.problem: 'It told you everything. Slow turn: speed ... Backward: float.' oversells the line. DRIVE_R spins backward at 4 rev/s, MISS at 5 and CHIP at 6. The drive and the chip line look almost the same. The chip floats because its spin is large compared with its low speed: spin ratio about 0.30 against 0.13 for DRIVE_R. Its 45 deg launch also helps. The spin rate alone does not decide it (Goff and Carre 2012, https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/98035/1/1-s2.0-S1877705812016414-main.pdf). Knuckle spin data: 0.9 vs 4.0 rev/s, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877705812016487.
issues.fix: Narration: 'And that line? It told you everything. Slow turn on a fast ball: speed. Sideways: bend. Forward: dive. Backward on a slow ball: float.' Visual beats: 'Ball 1 rolls slowly backward on a fast, flat flight icon.' and 'Ball 4 rolls backward on a slow, high-arc icon.'

issues.problem: 'Your leg's final whip is faster than a blink' applies the 70 ms to Tavi's volley. The verification says the 70 ms comes from full-power kicks at a STILL ball by 20 elite adults. Nobody has measured volley timing, so the line must say 'in a full-power kick' (volley mechanism_errors, step 3; https://drantoniopetrolo.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/KINEMATIC-DETERMINANTS-OF-THE-INSTEP-SOCCER-KICK-IN-ELITE-ADULT-SOCCER-PLAYERS_A-SYSTEMATIC-REVIEW.pdf). The blink comparison needs a source. A blink takes 0.1-0.4 s (BioNumbers 100706, https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=100706).
issues.fix: Narration: 'In a full-power kick, the leg's final whip is faster than a blink. But in that time, the ball falls more than its own width.' facts_used, add: 'A blink takes about 0.1-0.4 s (BioNumbers 100706).'

issues.problem: The visual 'The swing starts as the ball passes above it [the knee-height line]' puts the start of the whip at the contact height. That is about 70 ms too late. In the DROP sim, the ball is still about 0.36 m above the contact point when the whip must start. This is the key teaching beat, so the timing must show the real gap.
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'Start the swing while the ball is still above your knee.' A dashed knee-height line marks contact. The final whip starts while the ball is still about 36 cm above it, about one and a half ball widths.'

issues.problem: 'A thin cone from ball to goal shows the small set of angles that score' is wrong. The straight cone from the ball to the goal spans about -1.4 to +7.3 deg. The take-off angles that score point ABOVE the bar, because the ball falls on the way: about 12-21 deg at 72 km/h with no spin. The window is about 8 deg wide (volley safe list, model). If a viewer copies the drawn cone, the shot goes into the grass. The verification says 'close the face' means do not launch too steeply, not launch down.
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'From the edge of the box, the whole goal hides behind it.' The fist moves over the goal and covers it from the grass to the bar. Then a second thin cone of the same width tilts up above the bar: the take-off angles that score. Label: 'aim high, it falls'.'

issues.problem: (1) 'Biggest mistake?' ranks the mistakes, and no source does that. The failed-volley study (Sugi 2020, https://commons.nmu.edu/isbs/vol38/iss1/151/) names bottom-of-ball contact, an upright foot and less hip turn-in, not power. (2) 'hit the top half', with 'The top half of the ball glows green', goes further than the sources. US Youth Soccer says 'at or slightly above' the middle line (https://www.usyouthsoccer.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/160/2023/09/2017-Skills-School-Manual.pdf). A strike well into the top half with a forward-tilted face sends the ball down. The model needs the ball to leave 10-20 deg UP.
issues.fix: Narration: 'Classic mistake? Smashing it. A harder shot arrives sooner, so gravity has less time to pull it down. Same angle, harder, higher. Fix: nose over knee, knee over ball, hit it on or just above the middle. Clean beats hard.' Visual beat: 'A green band glows on and just above the middle of the ball. The bottom of the ball glows red.'

issues.problem: 'Volley it at the top of the bounce' uses the wrong word. By the verified England Football definition, a ball hit after it bounces is a half-volley: 'If it bounces before the player connects with it, or they hit it on the bounce, it's classed as a half volley' (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2022/Different-finishing-techniques-in-football).
issues.fix: Narration: 'Solo drill: drop the ball near a wall. Half-volley it at the top of the bounce, where it hangs like a soap bubble. Keep every shot under the tape. Now, for real. Under the bar.'

issues.problem: The floppy-ankle half says 'The ball rolls away with a short arrow'. That makes a loose ankle look very costly. In a kicking machine, a locked ankle gave only about 4% more ball speed (drive safe list, Peacock thesis https://vuir.vu.edu.au/37861/1/PEACOCK,%20James-Final%20Thesis_nosignature.pdf). The -15% on the next beat is about contact position (toes), not ankle looseness. Viewers can mix the two.
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'It folds, and the hit leaks away.' Left: at impact the toes are pushed further down and the hinge folds. Orange leak puffs escape. The ball's arrow is only a little shorter than on the right.' Keep the '-15%' only on the toe-contact beat, with the label '-15% (toe hit)'.

issues.problem: 'So aim about three metres outside your target' has no distance. The 2.7 m holds only from 20 m. Drift grows with the square of distance, so from 10 m it is only about 0.7 m (curler safe list; my run gives 0.67 m at 10 m).
issues.fix: Narration: 'From twenty metres, aim about three metres outside your target, and point your standing foot there.'

issues.problem: 'So that blink decides everything' calls a 9-10 ms contact a blink. A real blink is 0.1-0.4 s, 10-40 times longer (BioNumbers 100706). s14 then uses the blink as the LONGER yardstick against the 70 ms whip, so the two scenes clash. Also, the stopwatch stops at 0.010 s, but the shot shown is a laces kick, and the drive safe number is about 9 ms.
issues.fix: Narration: 'What went wrong? Your foot touches the ball for about a hundredth of a second. After that, it's on its own. So that instant decides everything.' Visual beat: 'HUD stopwatch (JetBrains Mono) creeps from 0.000 to 0.009 s.'

issues.problem: 'the face tilts forward, and the ball stays low' does not match the VOLLEY path. VOLLEY peaks at about 2.65 m, above the bar, and then dives to about 1.8 m at the line. 'Low' tells viewers to launch flat. From knee height, a flat 90 km/h volley hits the grass 5-7 m out (volley mechanism_errors).
issues.fix: Narration: 'Your laces are a tennis racket. Knee over the ball, toes down: the face tilts forward, and the ball stays under the bar. Lean back: the face tilts up.'

issues.problem: 'Swing level, and forward spin comes almost free' states the rigid-ball estimate as fact. The verification keeps that estimate at low confidence: 'the real spin can differ', and no volley spin has been measured. It asks for the wording 'can come almost for free'.
issues.fix: Narration: 'The falling ball slides down your laces, grips, and rolls forward over the top. Swing level, and forward spin can come almost free.'

issues.problem: EASY uses Cd 0.27 and SMASH uses Cd 0.25. So the 'same angle, only harder' demo changes two things at once. With Cd 0.27, SMASH still crosses at about 2.99 m after 0.76 s (my run), so the point holds with one variable.
issues.fix: physics_sim: 'Both balls from 16 m, contact 0.4 m, no spin, 18 deg up, Cd 0.27. EASY: 20 m/s (72 km/h), about 1.52 m at the line after about 0.95 s: goal. SMASH: 25 m/s (90 km/h), about 2.99 m after about 0.76 s: over.'

issues.problem: In the bowling-ball and ping-pong inset, the mass ratio is about 2600:1. That ratio makes the small ball leave at almost twice the striker's speed. A real kick has an effective foot mass of 1.7-2.1 kg, about 4-5 times the ball, and gives about 1.35 times the foot speed for a skilled adult. Young players get only 1.0-1.2 times (drive verification, https://www.jssm.org/mobile/fulltextmobile.php?id=jssm-06-154.xml).
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'Inset: a heavy trolley, about four times the ball's weight, bumps a ball, which leaves a little faster than the trolley. Back in X-ray, the ball leaves with a slightly longer arrow than the foot's arrow.'

issues.problem: 'Left side' and 'Right side' are correct only when the ball flies toward the top of the frame. If the top view shows the ball flying to screen-right, the with-flow side is screen-top, and the beats point at the wrong sides. The physics in the scene is correct: the with-flow side holds the air longer, the wake swings right and the ball moves left. The pressure story avoids the Bernoulli-only error.
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'Air rushes past the ball like a crowd.' Top view, ball flying toward the top of the frame. Hundreds of #7FB8FF particles with dot eyes stream from top to bottom past it.'

issues.problem: 'The ball clears the bar by about 0.6 m' uses the ball centre (3.06 m) minus 2.44 m. The bottom of the ball is at about 2.95 m, so it clears the bar line by about 0.5 m. The sim value itself is correct: my run gives 3.06 m at 1.05 s and lands at 29.8 m.
issues.fix: Visual beat: 'Over the bar.' The ball clears the bar by about half a metre and drops over the fence into the car park. A faint car alarm chirps once.'

issues.problem: 'Toes locked' mixes two cues. The verified cue is toes down and ankle locked (drive safe list; US Youth Soccer manual).
issues.fix: Narration: 'So, the first shot again. Knee over the ball. Toes down, ankle locked. Through the middle.'

issues.problem: Tense slips from present to past on the punchline. Every other line is present tense.
issues.fix: Replace "Chalk didn't even move." with "Chalk doesn't even move."

issues.problem: Coach: a 14-year-old alone on a pitch at ten at night is a habit parents and clubs will object to. An earlier hour keeps the mood and loses the worry.
issues.fix: Replace "Ten at night." with "Nine at night." In s23, replace "Half past ten." with "Half past nine." Move the stand clock hands to match in both scenes.

issues.problem: The hook shows a problem but makes no promise. An impatient viewer does not know what they get if they keep watching.
issues.fix: After "Or none at all." add: "By lights out, you'll score this shot." It also plants the s23 "Lights out." callback.

issues.problem: "That blink" names a 0.01 s contact. A real blink is 10 to 40 times longer. s14 then says the 0.07 s whip is "faster than a blink". A sharp kid catches the contradiction.
issues.fix: Replace "So that blink decides everything." with "So that tiny moment decides everything."

issues.problem: In audio, "then brakes" sounds like "then breaks". A kid hears that the thigh breaks.
issues.fix: Replace "The thigh swings, then brakes, and flings the shin." with "The thigh swings, then stops hard, and flings the shin forward."

issues.problem: "Flies off faster" does not say faster than what. The s03 question was about the foot, so the answer must name the foot.
issues.fix: Replace "Your leg is far heavier, so the ball flies off faster." with "Your leg is far heavier than the ball, so the ball bounces off faster than your foot."

issues.problem: "Hit with your toes" sounds like a toe-poke. It comes right after "toes down", so kids can mix the two cues.
issues.fix: Replace "Hit with your toes, and you lose about fifteen percent of your speed." with "Hit too near your toes, and the ball loses about fifteen percent of its speed."

issues.problem: Coach: "plant" appears only here. s12 and s14 say "standing foot". Pick one term. "Beside" also gives no direction for the foot.
issues.fix: Replace "So plant beside the ball. Plant behind it, and your foot is already rising." with "So put your standing foot next to the ball, toes pointing at the goal. Put it behind the ball, and your foot is already rising."

issues.problem: "The line turns slowly." has no why. The kid does not learn why slow spin is good.
issues.fix: Replace "The line turns slowly." with "The line turns slowly. Almost all your effort went into speed."

issues.problem: Coach and safety: "Lock it" does not say what "it" is. The spoken drill says "drive ten balls" at a wall with no power limit. The safety line is on screen only, and kids do not read it. "About ten metres" is hard to measure, and most solo players do not own ten balls. Club practice often has no wall.
